transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-02-23 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Moreno (Redwood SE), Rina Kapoor (CTO, Sandbar), Alex Chen (ML Eng), Marcus Lee (Platform)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
- Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for streaming NLU feature. Primary goals: p95 latency < 350ms for streaming responses at 20 concurrent users (approx 200 tokens/sec overall), steady-state throughput and graceful fallback. Concerned about cold starts, KV cash (transcript artifact), and network egress.

Topics:
- p95 targets and what they mean for streaming interactive use-cases
- concurrency model, batching, and token/sec shaping
- benchmark plan: token/sec tests, burst-surge, prefix caching
- security: SOC 2, KMS, SSO/SAML, VPC routing
- next steps and pilot proposal

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Samir (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we have about 45, 48 minutes, we'll try to run through your traffic profile and then jules will do the technical deep dive. can you start with a quick recap of what you're building?
[00:00:18] Rina (Sandbar CTO): sure thanks samir, hi all. we're building a realtime summarization + assistant for our publisher clients, it's streaming responses, lots of short prompts but long context, so token flow is kind of spiky. primary metric for us is p95 stream latency under load, target is 300 to 350ms for interactive UI.
[00:00:36] Alex (Sandbar ML): yeah and to add, we have bursts during publishing windows, like 200 concurrent editor sessions for a short period, otherwise steady 20-30 concurrency. token/sec per session varies, typically 5-15 tokens/sec but peak bursts push more.
[00:00:50] Samir: perfect, that's the sort of shape jules and i were hoping to see. jules, want to frame how redwood approaches streaming p95 and concurrency?
[00:00:56] Jules (Redwood SE): yeah absolutely. so two things to keep in mind, the runtime's continuous-batching + kv cache helps for repeated prefixes, and streaming p95 depends a lot on sequence length distribution, but also on how you shape tokens per second. we typically recommend a p95 target mapping exercise: if your average generation is 60 tokens and you need p95 < 350ms, we'll size either dedicated pool or hosted route accordingly.
[00:01:19] [00:01:20] Marcus (Sandbar Platform): quick q — when you say dedicated pool, how isolated is network egress? we have strict egress rules and need VPC peering or on-prem options.
[00:01:29] Jules: dedicated gives isolated GPU pools and optional VPC peering for the control plane; private (VPC/on-prem) gives full customer-managed networking. we can also provide a private control plane in your cloud region.
[00:01:40] Rina: and do you have metrics on cold starts for hosted? we saw one vendor had a 1.2s cold start for streaming which is a dealbreaker.
[00:01:47] Samir: yeah that's common. our hosted fleet uses warm pooling and fast model warmup paths; typical cold-start for large models in hosted is around 200-400ms until first tokens for streaming, but we recommend dedicated if you need strict SLOs and guaranteed warm workers.
[00:02:03] [00:02:10] Alex: can you explain what you mean by "warm pooling" — is it model pinned or container pinned?
[00:02:14] Jules: good question. we warm at the model variant + kernel path level; so workers maintain KV cache slots and tokenization ready state. for high-SLA customers we pin model instances in dedicated pools to minimize variance. there's also prefix caching and continuous batching to reduce per-token overhead.
[00:02:32] [00:02:38] Alex: and how does batching impact latency for streaming? last vendor said batching always increases tail latency.
[00:02:43] Jules: batching can increase latency if you wait to fill big batches; our runtime uses latency SLO-aware batching — essentially small windows and eager flush for streaming so you get the cost benefits when traffic is dense but we don't unduly increase p95 for interactive flows. it's tunable per-route.
[00:03:01] Rina: our target p95 is non-negotiable in Prod. if you can't hit it on hosted we want to understand the delta for dedicated and private. what's the usual multiplier?
[00:03:10] Samir: rough rule of thumb: hosted best-effort with warm pools can hit near-dedicated performance for many workloads, but for guaranteed p95 at scale add 10-25% margin. dedicated reduces jitter and variance — you'll see tighter p95s especially under burst. private (on-prem) is most deterministic but needs more ops.
[00:03:27] Marcus: curious about cost tradeoffs — if we run a pilot, what's the minimal footprint to evaluate streaming p95?
[00:03:35] Jules: for a pilot we usually spin up a small dedicated pool, e.g., 2-4 GPUs depending on model size, and run token/sec assays with your prompt set. that demonstrates latency profile and lets us tune batching/cache. pricing for pilot is discounted and credited if you convert.
[00:03:51] [00:03:58] Alex: about token/sec benchmarking — do you provide scripts? we want to replay real traffic shape not just synthetic constant rate.
[00:04:05] Samir: yes we have a benchmark repo and a template that can replay variable traffic shapes, bursts, and prefix reuse. i'll send that after.
[00:04:12] Rina: great. also security checkpoints — SOC 2 is mandatory, and keys must be in our KMS for private deploys. how's redwood handle KMS and audit logs?
[00:04:22] Jules: for hosted we integrate with our enterprise KMS connectors and provide audit logs, for private you manage keys fully. we can provide paper trail for encryption at rest and in transit, plus SSO/SAML and RBAC. we'll attach our security pack.
[00:04:36] [00:04:44] Marcus: network side — do you support asymmetric routing or egress via transit gateway? our infra team needs peering options and also want to avoid double egress charges.
[00:04:51] Samir: we support VPC peering and transit gateway patterns in major clouds, and can do region-local endpoints to limit cross-region egress. we'll need to map your AWS account setup.
[00:05:03] Alex: back to benchmarks — can you walk through an example output we should expect from a token/sec sweep? like how do you present p50/p95/p99 and token/sec curves?
[00:05:11] Jules: sure. our benchmark report includes per-token latency distributions, latency over time, cumulative token throughput, and memory/GPU utilization. for streaming we show time-to-first-token and per-chunk latency, plus tail plots at p50/p95/p99 and percent of requests meeting SLOs. we'll include CSVs and Grafana panels.
[00:05:32] [00:06:00] Rina: example scenario — 20 steady sessions @ 10 tokens/sec, with 200-token context, p95 target 350ms. can you ballpark concurrency and GPU sizing?
[00:06:10] Jules: ballpark depends on model and quantization. for a medium open model quantized to int8 on A100-class hardware you might get X tokens/sec per GPU; for your numbers rough guess: 20 sessions * 10 tps = 200 tokens/sec, a single well-configured GPU could handle that with headroom if you have caching and batching, but for burst you want another GPU for redundancy. we'll run real tests for exact.
[00:06:32] Marcus: you said quantization — do you do automated Q8/Q4 suggestions? we worry about quality regressions.
[00:06:38] Jules: yes, Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles by workload and includes quality regression checks against your eval set. we can tie regression alerts to a prompt suite. for pilot we'll recommend a profile that balances cost and quality and measure delta.
[00:06:53] [00:07:15] Alex: what's the fallback story if a model variant is out of capacity during a surge? do you do automated downgrade to a smaller model?
[00:07:20] Samir: we support smart routing and fallbacks — policy-driven. you can route by cost/latency/region and set automatic fallback to a compatible model variant. e.g., switch to a quantized or smaller model with preserved output semantics. team can define rollback rules.
[00:07:35] Rina: any known gotchas for streaming with very long contexts? we often push 5k-10k token contexts.
[00:07:42] Jules: long contexts increase KV cache pressure and per-token compute; it can increase variance in p95. techniques: prefix pruning, rolling window strategies, and memmap-friendly kernels. we also recommend evaluating split-encoder patterns if you're doing heavy retrieval + generation.
[00:07:58] [00:08:25] Marcus: rate limiting and quotas — does redwood have token-level throttles per API key? we need per-customer quotas and hard SLOs.
[00:08:32] Samir: yes token-level quotas, rate limits, per-route policies and realtime cost/latency dashboards.
[00:08:40] Alex: for the pilot tests do you simulate frontend jitter and variable network latencies? we get lots of client-side variability.
[00:08:48] Jules: we can incorporate client-side jitter in the replay harness. it's important because client RTT amplifies perceived p95. for internal SLOs we separate network vs compute latency in reports.
[00:08:59] [00:09:20] Rina: i want to call out data residency — some publishers require EU-only. can dedicated be region-locked?
[00:09:27] Samir: yes; dedicated pools can be provisioned in specific regions and for private you can keep everything in your VPC. we also support data retention controls and per-tenant logging.
[00:09:37] Marcus: is there an audit trail for per-token access? auditors ask for fine-grain logs sometimes.
[00:09:44] Jules: we provide request-level logs with redaction options, and you can integrate into your SIEM; note heavy logging can increase costs, we can sample.
[00:09:55] [00:10:10] Alex: for the benchmark template, what parameters do you need? list them maybe?
[00:10:15] Samir: we'll ask for: prompt set (typical, edge), token length distribution, concurrency profile, burst windows, auth pattern, and desired p95 target.
[00:10:25] Rina: timeline wise — we want results within two weeks to inform our Q2 runbook. feasible?
[00:10:31] Samir: yes if you provide prompt sets and traffic shape this week we can run a pilot next week and deliver a report within 7-10 business days.
[00:10:41] [00:11:00] Alex: last technical — how do you measure streaming p95? chunk-level or end-to-end? sometimes vendors report time-to-first-chunk as opposed to completion latency.
[00:11:09] Jules: we report multiple metrics: time-to-first-token, per-chunk latency distribution, and effective completion latency for the full response. we recommend focusing on time-to-first-token for UI interactivity and per-chunk p95 for continued streaming smoothness.
[00:11:28] Rina: great. let's do a short recap and next steps.
[00:11:33] Samir: recap: we'll send benchmark template + scripts; jules will prepare lab environment for a 2h streaming p95 run; sandbar to provide prompt set + traffic shape; security pack will be shared; we'll propose dedicated pool pilot pricing.
[00:11:48] Marcus: can you include an explicit runbook for the pilot so our infra team can approve peering quickly?
[00:11:54] Samir: yes we'll include network runbook and list of IAM roles and peering steps.
[00:12:00] [00:12:30] Alex: one more question — do you have example dashboards for token-level cost breakdown? our CFO will want to see economics.
[00:12:36] Jules: yes the console has token-level cost and latency breakdowns by route and model; we'll attach screenshots and a sample export.
[00:12:46] Rina: okay thanks everyone, that was helpful. i'll expect the template and security pack.
[00:12:52] Samir: thanks rina, thanks team we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the lab demo.
[00:13:00] [00:35:00 - 00:47:45] Appendix: later part of the call covered details about model variants (gpt-like open models vs finetuned internal models), pricing tiers for dedicated pools, and an operational checklist. there was short crosstalk about integration timeline with their CMS at 00:36:12 where a few words got garbled ("KV cash" mentioned).
